Survivors often couldn't be trusted, but this one held himself with the conviction of a man who knew full well what he was offering and still chose it. Fascinating. He breached the gap between them with barely a half step, locking Jake's outstretched hand in a crushing grip that sent sparks licking up his arm like a promise of things to come. Jake gasped through clenched teeth, but didn’t pull away. Good. Herman pulled him in slightly, enough for Jake to smell the sharp ozone on his breath, feel the faint tremor in the air around him from the static charge crawling through his veins. His voice lowered to a threatening growl as he towered over the smaller man. "Should you go back on your end of this, I will personally take every single one of your people who come through my domain. I will send them back to you broken and charred after slowly extracting every conscious thought they have ever had from their hollowed-out husk of a mind with my bare hands . Not a single one will be spared until I have taken what is owed to me. And every single one will return to the Fog with their last living thought being the knowledge that you did this to them. Are we clear?" Jake's defiant glare cracked ever so slightly, a sheen of terror passing over his eyes. He nodded briefly, and Herman felt the heartbeat under his grip quicken. Excellent . The fear would keep him honest. Besides, what he had planned was much more fun when the subject was trying to hold it together and failing beautifully. Deal accepted. Herman loomed at the far end of the hallway, keeping just enough distance that his terror radius wouldn’t bleed into the survivors’ ears. Close enough to monitor. Not close enough to break the illusion of choice . He wasn’t about to let Jake out of his sight. The man had proven himself a persistent thorn, and while Herman now had leverage, he wasn’t fool enough to underestimate desperation. If Jake decided to bolt, he’d be on him in a second. But for now, he watched. Jake and Claudette were hunched over the last generator, working in tandem, both trying to pretend that there wasn’t a killer watching their every move from the shadowed end of the corridor. Jake's relief was subtle but clear — he was glad Meg had gone for the gate. She wouldn’t have kept to the plan otherwise. Too stubborn. Too loud. Too righteous . He’d have sent both girls on ahead if he could have, but this was much faster with two. Even from his perch, Herman could see Jake’s shoulders trembling. Not from exhaustion — but from sheer effort. The restraint it took to stay put under this kind of pressure was commendable, in a way. A lesser man would’ve cracked already. He had sent the cop back first — Jake had led him back to their hiding place before circling back to the generator. He had put up no resistance, not after so much personalized attention, and only really showed any spark of consciousness when the hook went through him, letting out a quiet, pained sound and grabbing at the metal moments before the Entity's claws ran him through and took him for Her meal. Satisfying to watch, at the least, even if he didn't have enough in him to scream the way they usually do. Herman could feel the Entity's pressure ease up on his mind slightly at the offering as well, leaving him feeling much less strained. His quota wasn't quite there yet, but at least he wasn't at risk of receiving Her full attention for a while now. That was far more valuable to him right now. He needed Her to leave him be for a while. This one... was personal. Down the hall, the generator flared to life. Jake gave Claudette a firm, reassuring nod — go — and she didn’t hesitate. She slipped past him, creeping along the wall as she passed the Doctor, shrinking away from the slow, gleaming grin he offered her in return. At least someone in this trial had a healthy sense of fear. In the distance, rust screamed and metal groaned — sharp and strained under years of neglect — marking the gate’s slow, shuddering rise. The Fog shifted, its pressure subtly relaxing as the girls crossed the threshold. Gone. He sighed in mild annoyance, never liking to simply allow an escape. He had contemplated chasing them out, at least making them earn it before pulling back to watch them scramble across the threshold, but the collapse was a limited window and he didn't want to waste a second of it having to navigate back from the gate. Jake had already moved to the rotunda by the time Herman rejoined him, standing among the Entity's vein-like cracks that spread across the floor as the timer ticked down in their minds. The lights overhead cast a halo around him — arms curled tight around his chest, feet locked in place. It was nearly picture perfect, the way he stood there defiantly resisting the natural instinct to flee. Herman paused to admire the sight. The survivor hadn’t run. Hadn’t faltered. No tricks. No tantrum. He had actually meant it . Herman respected that. It would make this all the more rewarding. A wide grin peeled across his face as he stepped into the light, current dancing eagerly along his shoulders, snapping from nearby chairs like leashed lightning. His voltage was already rising — amped higher than it had been in months. Four minutes. More than enough. He raised a hand towards Jake, sparks licking across fingers with sharp, deliberate arches. “When you see Mr. Richter, do be sure to pass along my regards.” The lights flared —
